note: The score measures how well a pitch's claims hold up; it does not predict success. Weights fixed before any outcome was seen.
not_measured: The team (which VCs rank as the most important factor), market timing, product quality and valuation fairness are not scored.

A.name: Evidence balance
A.basis: Overly high claims are dismissed as cheap talk and penalised for credibility; classic pitch lies ('no one is doing what we're doing', 'conservative' projections) are exactly what public evidence checks. Contradicted claims count double.

sources.title: Kleinert (2023), Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice
sources.quote: promising overly high growth ambitions might backfire for entrepreneurs—dismissed as cheap talk and even penalized due to investors’ credibility concerns

sources.title: Kawasaki & Reichert (2006), The Top Ten Lies of Entrepreneurs
sources.quote: every pitch contains at least three or four of these lies

B.name: Specificity
B.basis: Only concrete claims (numbers, named customers, dates) can be checked; checkable, costly signals turn ambition into credible signals. This is about checkability, not writing style: style alone hardly matters for commercial pitches.

sources.title: Kleinert (2023), Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice
sources.quote: Such costly signals can serve as credibility buffers and transform high ambitions from cheap talk into credible signals.

sources.title: Parhankangas & Renko (2017), Journal of Business Venturing (caveat)
sources.quote: boost the success of social campaigns, but hardly matter for commercial campaigns

C.name: Consistency
C.basis: Numbers that can't all be true, or a founder contradicting the deck or themselves live, are the cheapest red flags to detect; inflated projections are usually exposed by the deck's own arithmetic.

sources.title: Kawasaki & Reichert (2006), The Top Ten Lies of Entrepreneurs
sources.quote: An entrepreneur’s projections are never conservative.

D.name: Verifiable core
D.basis: Investors verify the core of a deal through diligence and references before investing; a pitch whose most load-bearing claims can't be checked asks for more trust.

sources.title: Gompers, Gornall, Kaplan, Strebulaev (2020), How Do Venture Capitalists Make Decisions?
sources.quote: the average firm spends 118 hours on due diligence over that period and the average firm calls 10 references
